additional_requirements: Functioning is not markedly impaired apart from the impact of the delusion(s) or its ramifications

S019.name: Delusions
S019.description: Fixed beliefs that do not change easily, even in the face of contradictory evidence.

subtypes.Persecutory Delusions: The false belief that one is being harmed or monitored by other people or organizations.
subtypes.Referential Delusions: The conviction that ordinary events, remarks, or behaviors have specific relevance to oneself.
subtypes.Grandiose Delusions: The false belief that one possesses special abilities, power, or fame.
subtypes.Erotomanic Delusions: The false belief that another person is in love with or has affection for them.
subtypes.Nihilistic Delusions: A destructive or negative conviction that the world is ending or that a major catastrophe will occur.
subtypes.Somatic Delusions: The baseless conviction that there is a serious abnormality with one's body or organs.
subtypes.Jealous Delusions: The conviction that one's spouse or romantic partner is being unfaithful without sufficient evidence.

symptom.disease_info: Delusional disorder is characterized by one or more persistent, non-bizarre or somewhat plausible delusions lasting at least one month, in the absence of prominent hallucinations, disorganized thought, or marked functional decline typical of schizophrenia. Outside the delusional themes, individuals often appear relatively intact, with preserved cognition, affect, and daily functioning, which can delay detection and treatment. Onset is typically in mid-to-late adulthood and may follow psychosocial stressors, interpersonal conflicts, or situations that can be misinterpreted and woven into a fixed false belief. It is distinguished from mood and psychotic disorders by the circumscribed nature of the beliefs, minimal other psychotic features, and relatively stable overall functioning.

patient.personality: Jose is a calm, disciplined, and highly skilled welder who takes pride in his craftsmanship, competitiveness, and devotion to family and practical routines.
patient.stressor: Roughly two years ago, Jose experienced a minor workplace accident where he briefly lost consciousness after being struck by a falling piece of metal, followed by several weeks of headaches and dizziness that were evaluated in the emergency department and deemed without serious findings. Although he initially returned to work, he remained uneasy about his health, reading articles and watching documentaries about long-term effects of head injuries and industrial exposures, and he began to fixate on the idea that something had been missed or was being hidden from him. Routine follow-up visits and normal test results did not reassure him; instead, he increasingly interpreted medical explanations and paperwork errors as signs that doctors, his employer, and even the workers’ compensation insurer were concealing a serious condition or using him as part of some undisclosed study. Over the course of a year, this belief hardened despite his wife’s attempts to accompany him to appointments and clarify what was said, and only after he started refusing recommended procedures, arguing with supervisors about supposed hidden health risks, and his family doctor noted how immovable his ideas had become did they convince him to accept a referral to psychiatric care.
patient.chief_complaint: “I keep holding on to these ideas about my health and what the doctors and company are doing, and nobody can convince me they’re wrong.”

S019.name: Delusions
S019.description: Fixed beliefs that do not change easily, even in the face of contradictory evidence.
S019.manifestation: No matter how many times the doctors tell me my scans and blood work are fine, I can’t shake this feeling that they found something serious in my head after the accident and that my boss, the hospital, and the insurance people are all working together to cover it up and just keep me going like some kind of test subject.
